'''Pavel Samuilovich Urysohn'''  (in [[Russian language|Russian]]: {{lang|ru|Па́вел Самуи́лович Урысо́н}}; 3 February 1898 – 17 August 1924) was a [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] [[mathematician]] who is best known for his contributions to the theory of topological dimension, and for developing [[Urysohn's metrization theorem]] and [[Urysohn's lemma]], both of which are fundamental results in [[topology]]. He also constructed what is now called the [[Urysohn universal space]]<ref>Miroslav Hušek, ''Urysohn universal space, its development and Hausdorff's approach'', Topology and its Applications, Volume 155, Issue 14, 2008, Pages 1493-1501 doi:10.1016/j.topol.2008.03.020</ref> and his name is also commemorated in the terms [[Fréchet–Urysohn space]], [[Menger–Urysohn dimension]] and [[Urysohn integral equation]]. He and [[Pavel Alexandrov]] formulated the modern definition of [[Compact space|compactness]] in 1923.

== Biography ==
Pavel Urysohn was born in [[Odesa]] in 1898.<ref name="mathshistory">{{Cite web |title=Pavel Urysohn - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Urysohn/ |access-date=2023-07-17 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref> His mother died when he was little, and he entered the care of his father and sister. The family moved to [[Moscow]] in 1912, where Urysohn completed his secondary education.<ref name="mathnet">{{Cite web |title=A. V. Arkhangel'skii, V. M. Tikhomirov, "Pavel Samuilovich Urysohn (1898–1924)", Uspekhi Mat. Nauk, 53:5(323) (1998), 5–26; Russian Math. Surveys, 53:5 (1998), 875–892 |url=https://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?wshow=paper&jrnid=rm&paperid=67&option_lang=eng |access-date=2023-07-17 |website=www.mathnet.ru}}</ref> While still at school, he worked at [[Shanyavsky Moscow City People's University|Shanyavsky University]] on an experimental project on X-ray radiation and was supervised by [[Petr Lazarev]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Arkhangelskii |first=A V |author-link=Alexander Arhangelskii |last2=Tikhomirov |first2=V M |date=1998-10-31 |title=Pavel Samuilovich Urysohn (1898-1924) |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1070/rm1998v053n05abeh000067 |journal=Russian Mathematical Surveys |volume=53 |issue=5 |pages=875–892 |doi=10.1070/rm1998v053n05abeh000067 |issn=0036-0279|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="encyclopediacom">{{Cite web |title=Uryson, Pavel Samuilovich {{!}} Encyclopedia.com |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/science/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/uryson-pavel-samuilovich |access-date=2023-07-17 |website=www.encyclopedia.com}}</ref>

At that time, Urysohn's interests lay predominantly in physics. Urysohn enrolled at the Moscow State University in 1915 and earned his Bachelor of Science in 1919.<ref name="mathshistory" /><ref name="mathnet" /> There he attended the lectures of [[Nikolai Luzin]] and [[Dmitri Egorov|Dimitri Egorov]], which made him turn his attention to mathematics.<ref name="encyclopediacom" /><ref name="mathnet" /><ref name="mathshistory" /> Between 1919 and 1921, Urysohn completed a doctorate on integral equations under the supervision of Luzin.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pavel Urysohn - The Mathematics Genealogy Project |url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=36446 |access-date=2023-07-17 |website=www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu}}</ref> He then became an assistant professor at [[Moscow State University|Moscow University]], and Egorov prompted him to start working in topology.<ref name="mathshistory" />&nbsp;

By 1922, Urysohn had given topological definitions to curve, surface, and dimension, and his work attracted the attention of many prominent European mathematicians.<ref name="mathshistory" /><ref name="encyclopediacom" /> In the summers of 1923 and 1924, Urysohn and his friend and fellow mathematician, [[Pavel Alexandrov|Pavel Aleksandrov]], traveled through France, Holland, and Germany, where they met [[David Hilbert]], [[Felix Hausdorff]], and [[L. E. J. Brouwer]].<ref name="mathshistory" /> The three European mathematicians were impressed by Urysohn's work and expressed their hopes that he would visit them again in subsequent years.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Arboleda |first=L. C. |date=1979-03-01 |title=Les Débuts de l'École Topologique Soviétique: Notes sur les Lettres de Paul S. Alexandroff et Paul S. Urysohn à Maurice Fréchet |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00776067 |journal=Archive for History of Exact Sciences |language=fr |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=73–89 |doi=10.1007/BF00776067 |issn=1432-0657|url-access=subscription }}</ref>&nbsp;

Urysohn and Aleksandrov were staying in a cottage in [[Brittany]], France, when Urysohn drowned at the age of 26 while swimming off the coast nearby [[Batz-sur-Mer]].<ref name="mathshistory" />

Urysohn's sister, Lina Neiman, wrote a memoir about his life and childhood. Not being a mathematician, she included in the book memorial articles about his mathematical works by [[Pavel Alexandrov]], [[Vadim Yefremovich|Vadim Efremovich]], [[Andrey Kolmogorov|Andrei Kolmogorov]], [[Lazar Lyusternik]], and [[Mark Krasnoselsky|Mark Krasnosel'skii]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Лина Нейман Радость открытия |url=http://www.ega-math.narod.ru/LSP/Neuman.htm |access-date=2023-07-17 |website=www.ega-math.narod.ru}}</ref>
